items.topic: Sundowning — reduce evening stimulation; calm routine; adequate lighting
items.stem: An older adult with dementia becomes more agitated and confused each late afternoon (sundowning). Which teaching best guides family caregiving?

options.text: Reduce evening stimulation (limit loud TV/chores), keep a calm routine, and use adequate lighting to lessen shadows and confusion
Schedule all medical appointments and baths late at night when agitation peaks
Argue firmly until the client accepts that the day is over
Keep the home dark after lunch so the client sleeps until morning

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax Fundamentals: reduce evening TV/stimulation, use calming activities, and address triggers; adequate evening lighting helps. OpenStax Psych: confusion often worse in evening (sundowning); calm communication and supportive environment.
rationales.B: Incorrect. OpenStax Fundamentals suggests scheduling demanding activities earlier when the person is more alert.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Arguing increases agitation; calm, simple communication is preferred.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Daylight exposure and adequate evening lighting help; prolonged darkness/shadows can worsen confusion.

items.topic: Metformin — hold around IV iodinated contrast; lactic acidosis risk
items.stem: A client taking metformin is scheduled for a radiologic procedure with IV iodinated contrast. Which teaching is most accurate?

options.text: Metformin is often held around IV contrast because contrast plus reduced kidney function can raise the risk of lactic acidosis; follow the provider/protocol hold and restart plan
Double the metformin dose the morning of contrast to protect the kidneys
Metformin never interacts with contrast dye, so no hold is ever needed
Replace metformin with a sulfonylurea only on the day of contrast and stop checking renal function

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax: contrast dye can increase lactic acidosis risk with metformin and reduced renal function; withhold per protocol around contrast. Merck: stop metformin temporarily before radiologic procedures requiring contrast agents; lactic acidosis risk.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Increasing the dose does not mitigate contrast-related risk and is unsafe.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Sources advise temporary hold around IV contrast in at-risk clients.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Arbitrary sulfonylurea swap without renal monitoring is not the recommended approach.

sources.title: 28.3 Oral Antidiabetic Drugs
sources.evidence: Contrast increases lactic acidosis risk with metformin and decreased renal function; withhold around contrast per eGFR/protocol guidance.

sources.section: Biguanides / Oral Antihyperglycemic Medications — metformin contrast hold
sources.evidence: Metformin: rare lactic acidosis; withhold during IV contrast and surgery; stop temporarily before contrast procedures.

items.topic: Dislodged chest tube — three-sided occlusive dressing; notify provider
items.stem: A client's chest tube accidentally pulls out of the insertion site. Which immediate action is best while calling for help/notifying the provider?

options.text: Cover the site with a sterile occlusive dressing taped on three sides (leave one side open) so air can escape and reduce tension pneumothorax risk
Tape an airtight dressing on all four sides with no vent and leave the client unobserved
Routinely clamp the remaining tubing for the rest of the shift without assessment
Push the contaminated tube back into the chest without sterile technique

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax Med-Surg: if chest tube dislodged, apply three-sided occlusive dressing to allow air escape. Open RN/NCBI: tape dressing on three sides to prevent tension pneumothorax; notify provider.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Fully sealed dressing can trap air and promote tension pneumothorax.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Routine clamping is not recommended due to tension pneumothorax risk.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Do not reinsert a contaminated tube; cover site and notify provider.

sources.title: 11.6 Disorders of the Lower Respiratory System: Pneumothorax
sources.evidence: If chest tube becomes dislodged, apply three-sided occlusive dressing allowing trapped air to escape while preventing more air from entering.

items.topic: Restraints — choose least restrictive option (mitts before wrist ties)
items.client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
items.stem: A nonviolent client repeatedly reaches for a peripheral IV. Alternatives have failed and a restraint order is obtained. Which choice best reflects least-restrictive practice?

options.text: Apply padded mitts first because they restrict grasping while preserving more extremity range of motion than wrist ties
Apply a vest restraint immediately for an IV-protection problem
Use the most restrictive device available so monitoring can be skipped
Restrain without trying alternatives because restraints are first-line for all IV sites

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax CNS: select least restrictive restraint; padded mitts are less restrictive than wrist ties for preventing tube dislodgement while preserving ROM. Open RN: hand mitts/soft wrists used for tube protection; alternatives first.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Vest restraints are more restrictive and not the least restrictive choice for IV protection.
rationales.C: Incorrect. More restrictive devices increase harm; monitoring remains required.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Restraints are used only when alternatives cannot meet safety needs.

items.topic: ECT — controlled seizure under anesthesia; temporary memory impairment possible
items.stem: A client with severe treatment-resistant depression is scheduled for ECT. Which teaching is most accurate?

options.text: ECT induces a controlled seizure under anesthesia/supportive care and may cause temporary confusion or memory impairment that often improves over time
ECT is delivered fully awake without any anesthesia because seizures are painless
ECT permanently erases all remote and recent memory in every client and is never used for depression
ECT replaces the need for any consent discussion because it is only a psychotherapy technique

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax: ECT uses electricity to create a controlled seizure, commonly for major depression. Merck: modern ECT under general anesthesia; confusion and memory impairment may occur acutely and often improve, though some retrograde amnesia can persist.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Merck: brief general anesthesia is used because the electrical current can cause muscle contractions and pain.
rationales.C: Incorrect. ECT is used for severe depression; memory effects are often temporary, not universal permanent total erasure.
rationales.D: Incorrect. ECT is a biological/brain-stimulation treatment requiring informed consent, not talk therapy alone.

sources.title: 2.5 Biological Theories and Therapies
sources.evidence: ECT uses electricity to stimulate targeted brain areas by creating a controlled seizure; commonly used to treat major depression.

sources.title: Depressive Disorders
sources.evidence: ECT under general anesthesia; confusion and memory impairment may occur acutely; much improves by 6 months; retrograde amnesia may persist.

items.jurisdiction_note: CNO / RHPA mandatory reporting of suspected sexual abuse of a patient by a nurse
items.topic: Ontario — nurse must report suspected sexual abuse of a patient by a nurse to CNO
items.stem: An Ontario nurse hears a patient's credible account that another nurse touched them in a sexual manner during care. What is the reporting obligation?

options.text: Report the suspected sexual abuse to the College of Nurses of Ontario (CNO) as required; a patient's account can constitute reasonable grounds
Wait indefinitely until a criminal conviction is obtained before any report is considered
Ignore the disclosure because consensual-appearing relationships with current patients are allowed
Post the patient's name and details on social media to warn the public

rationales.A: Correct. CNO: nurses are legally required to report suspected sexual abuse of a patient by a nurse to CNO. CNO Boundaries: under RHPA/HPPC, nurses must report reasonable grounds to suspect sexual abuse to the appropriate college; a client's account constitutes reasonable grounds. RHPA HPPC s.85.1: member shall report reasonable grounds that another member sexually abused a patient.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Reporting obligation does not wait for criminal conviction; report suspected sexual abuse promptly (within RHPA timelines).
rationales.C: Incorrect. Any sexual/romantic relationship with a patient is sexual abuse for regulated health professionals.
rationales.D: Incorrect. PHI must not be posted publicly; patient name in a CNO report requires written consent.

items.topic: High-alert meds — independent second-nurse dose verification (insulin/heparin)
items.stem: Before giving subcutaneous insulin, which leadership/safety practice best reduces high-alert medication error risk?

options.text: Have a second nurse independently verify the insulin type and dose (do not draw up until a witness is available per policy)
Skip verification because insulin is never classified as high-alert
Draw heparin into an insulin syringe to 'save time'
Ask an unlicensed visitor to confirm the dose from memory

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax Pharm: insulin/heparin are high-alert; a second nurse verifies the dose; do not draw up until a witness is available. OpenStax 3.2: double-check high-alert medication doses with another provider; ISMP high-alert drugs should have two-provider verification.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Insulin is a classic high-alert medication.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Never draw heparin into an insulin syringe.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Verification must be by a qualified provider/nurse per policy, not a visitor.
